clue.text: One of a pair Cinderella found relatively ugly

definitions.text: One of a pair Cinderella found relatively ugly

parts.words: One of a pair Cinderella found relatively ugly
parts.note: surface reading: someone Cinderella thought fairly unattractive, as compared with others; setter's reading: 'relatively' means by family relation, so this is one of the two Ugly Sisters of the pantomime, related to her by marriage

explanation.walkthrough: 'Relatively ugly' reads as 'somewhat ugly', but it means 'ugly and a relative': one of the pantomime's two Ugly Sisters.
explanation.definitionFit: In the fairy tale Cinderella's two ugly tormentors are daughters of her father's new wife, so each is related only through marriage.

clue.text: Little house thus supported in London

definitions.note: a pointer to a district in London

indicators.note: in a down entry what is supported sits on top, so 'thus' stands above the house

parts.note: HO is the short form of house

explanation.surface: A small house is propped up somewhere in the capital.
explanation.definitionFit: This district of the West End is famous for its restaurants, theatres and nightlife in the city centre.

clue.text: Bring in a vase, say

indicators.note: say means spoken out, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: an urn is a kind of vase

explanation.surface: Someone carries a vase indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent the two words sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring in money is to make it as wages or profit, an idiomatic synonym.

clue.text: Terrible scene out East — but not in India for instance

indicators.note: something terrible is in a bad way, so the letters are thrown into disorder
out means removed, so the compass letter is taken away

explanation.surface: A dreadful scene somewhere in the East, though not in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not in India' looks like an exclusion, but 'but not in' are letters, and India is the example in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: India occupies a large distinct landmass of Asia, the classic example of that geographical term.

clue.text: Duration of a photographer's exposure to a drug?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: shutter setting, how long the film is exposed

explanation.surface: A photographer may have been exposed to drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: Shutter setting governs how long light reaches the film, and amphetamine is known by the same slang word.

clue.text: Stamina can possibly continue to exist without it

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the phrase wraps round the reworked word
possibly suggests one of the arrangements the letters might take

explanation.surface: Staying power may let you go on without it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' here means outside, an old sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamina is the capacity to keep going through long physical or mental effort; the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Egghead said in Paris to supervise a journal

parts.note: the head of the word egg is its first letter

explanation.surface: A French intellectual is invited to run a learned periodical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Egghead' looks like one word for an intellectual, but it splits into egg and head.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversee the preparation and content of a publication as its editor is to perform that verb.

clue.text: Refusal to acknowledge record with comparatively weak sound

indicators.note: sound tells us to take the word as spoken, not as spelt

explanation.surface: A record with a feeble sound is disowned.
explanation.definitionFit: A statement denying responsibility or connection is a formal renunciation of a claim.

clue.text: Manufacturers' symbols for many a vessel hemmed in by winds

indicators.note: something hemmed in is surrounded on all sides by what encloses it

parts.note: the trades are the trade winds of the tropics

explanation.surface: Logos for lots of ships surrounded by gales.
explanation.definitionFit: Registered logos or names identify a maker's goods, which is what companies' brand emblems are.

clue.text: Mingling of certain players heard in rock?

definitions.note: strictly a mineral found in rocks such as granite

indicators.note: something heard is taken by its sound, not by its spelling

parts.note: a blend of horn players: brass instruments mingling

explanation.surface: Musicians mixing their sounds in a rock band.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock' looks like the music, which suits 'players'; it is the geology.
explanation.definitionFit: Hornblende is a dark mineral common in igneous and metamorphic stone, so it is loosely a kind of rock.

clue.text: Shere Khan'S territory in the latter half of Disney's film

indicators.note: the latter half of a word is its second half, so only those letters are kept

parts.note: Fantasia is the 1940 Disney film; its last four of eight letters are kept

explanation.surface: Where the tiger of The Jungle Book roams in the later part of the Disney cartoon.
explanation.walkthrough: The Jungle Book points at a Disney film, but the film needed is Fantasia.
explanation.definitionFit: Shere Khan is the tiger of Kipling's Jungle Book, set in India, so his home continent is the largest landmass.

clue.text: Dispensable, unlike oil in the plant!

parts.note: surface reading: a factory's machines cannot do without lubricating oil; setter's reading: the fragrant oil extracted from a plant is called essential oil, so something dispensable is its opposite

explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as a factory; it is a living plant, whose aromatic oils are called essential.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not required can be given up without loss, the exact meaning of dispensable.

clue.text: Dog given command in one Belloc novel

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new, so these letters are worked into a fresh order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A dog obeys an instruction found in a Hilaire Belloc story.
explanation.walkthrough: Strictly the setter's 'in' puts the command inside the jumbled one-plus-Belloc; the letters come out the same whichever way they are read.
explanation.definitionFit: This breed is the classic working sheepdog of the hill farms between Scotland and England.

clue.text: Continental friend with talent and good humour

explanation.surface: A European pal who is gifted and cheerful.
explanation.definitionFit: Friendliness and pleasant temper describe a genial disposition, which is what the noun names.

clue.text: Imprudent but undivided, by the sound of it

indicators.note: by the sound of it says to judge the word by how it is spoken

parts.note: indiscrete means not separated into parts

explanation.surface: Someone is rash yet wholehearted, apparently.
explanation.definitionFit: Being careless about what one reveals or does shows a lack of tact and caution, as rash behaviour does.

clue.text: Mum carries in weapon — a sign of distress

indicators.note: to carry something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within the other

explanation.surface: A mother carrying a weapon is a worrying sight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mum' looks like a mother; here it means silent.
explanation.definitionFit: A minute gun is a cannon fired once every sixty seconds, traditionally signalling a ship in trouble or a mourning.

clue.text: Grand language for writing notes in? Nonsense

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for grand

indicators.note: writing something into a word means setting it down inside that word
in says the musical letters go inside the language

parts.note: B, B and E are musical notes

explanation.surface: A fine tongue for composing music in, or just rubbish?
explanation.definitionFit: Meaningless jabber or unintelligible talk is drivel, so it means the same as rubbish speech.

clue.text: Gradually approaching a heath?

indicators.note: approaching means coming up next to, so one piece is set right before the other

parts.note: 'Eric, or Little by Little' is F. W. Farrar's Victorian school novel, and little by little means gradually

explanation.surface: Slowly getting nearer to an open moor.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue leans on the title of an old Victorian schoolboy story, 'Eric, or Little by Little'.
explanation.definitionFit: Erica is the botanical genus of heaths and heathers, so a single heath plant can be called by it.

clue.text: Article written by man about extraterrestrial visitor

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the man's name is read from its end

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece by some man reports a visitor from space.
explanation.definitionFit: A being from another planet who comes to Earth is the science-fiction sense of that noun.

clue.text: Food originally fried to feed some working with wood

indicators.note: feeding something puts it inside, so the letter goes into the group

parts.note: a bee is a gathering for communal work, as in a quilting bee

indicators.note: originally points to the origin, the very start, so the opening letter is kept

explanation.surface: Fried snacks are handed out to carpenters at work.
explanation.walkthrough: A bee is a social gathering for working together, like a spelling or quilting bee.
explanation.definitionFit: A thick slice of beef for grilling or frying is something to eat, so the general word covers it.

clue.text: Awkward position of nuns sheltering oddly naive characters

indicators.note: to shelter is to hold safely inside, so the letters go within the phrase

parts.note: where nuns are: in a convent

indicators.note: oddly picks the letters in odd-numbered places: first, third, fifth

explanation.surface: Nuns in a difficult spot take in some innocent people.
explanation.definitionFit: Something troublesome or badly timed causes difficulty, the same idea as clumsy and inconvenient.

clue.text: It's better than a magpie for the sort of man we feed!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: on a shooting target, the ring next to the bull, which scores more than a magpie, the ring outside it

explanation.walkthrough: A magpie looks like the bird; it is a target-shooting term for a hit in the second-outermost ring.
explanation.definitionFit: On a target the ring just outside the bull scores above a magpie; 'feeding the inner man' is a jocular idiom for eating.

clue.text: Indo-European bondsman with no English

indicators.note: with no means lacking, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: a bondsman is a serf or slave
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A European serf who speaks no English.
explanation.definitionFit: Slavic peoples speak languages in the Indo-European family, so a member of them fits the broad label.

clue.text: How this composer travelled from London to Essex?

parts.note: how you travelled: by some means
RD is the abbreviation for road, the way one travels

explanation.surface: Asking how an old composer got from the capital to his country home.
explanation.walkthrough: William Byrd, the Tudor composer, spent his last decades in Essex, so he would have gone by road.
explanation.definitionFit: William Byrd was the great English composer of church music under Elizabeth I, who settled in Essex.

clue.text: Mini-tempest producing a bit of news

indicators.note: producing means bringing out, so the letters are brought out from within the words

parts.note: found inside, from the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A storm in a teacup makes the papers.
explanation.definitionFit: A single short report in a newspaper or bulletin is a piece, a news story.

clue.text: Unusual novice with a by-line in — but not very often

indicators.note: something unusual is out of the ordinary, so the letters leave their ordinary order

parts.note: L for learner, as on L-plates

explanation.surface: An odd beginner journalist gets their name printed, but rarely.
explanation.walkthrough: L-plates mark a learner driver in Britain, so L is a novice.
explanation.definitionFit: Happening once every two years is a rare frequency, so the adverb is fairly glossed as seldom.

clue.text: Nevertheless it lost its tail, allegedly, in the Himalayas

definitions.note: a cryptic pointer: the thing that lives, allegedly, in the Himalayas

indicators.note: losing a tail means the final letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A creature, despite having lost its tail, is said to live among the high mountains.
explanation.definitionFit: The abominable snowman is a legendary ape-like beast said to roam Nepal and Tibet, though never proved.

clue.text: Extremely restrained, this love may be ephemeral

indicators.note: may be suggests what the letters could become if rearranged
the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the outside letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters of restrained

explanation.surface: A very reserved romance may not last.
explanation.definitionFit: Ephemeral means lasting only a brief time, like a mayfly; a fleeting affair is over quickly.
